lines: Last time, a directory listing turned out to be a terrible way to define a table — a reader could catch a write half done, with nothing to say it was wrong.
So replace it with something that can't lie like that: one file that never changes, plus a single pointer to whichever one is current.
Here's the puzzle. If that file is never, ever edited once it's written, how does the table's content actually move forward?
Does something quietly patch a few bytes inside it, or does the whole picture work differently?
answer: Nothing ever gets patched. A brand new file gets written describing the new state, and a pointer swings over to point at it.
The old file just sits there afterward, completely untouched — nobody ever has a reason to go back and change it.

lines: So what actually goes inside one of these files? Not a list of what changed since last time — the entire table.
Every single data file that belongs to the table, right now, all in one place, readable start to finish with nothing else to consult.
And committing a change is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it. Write the new version out completely, then flip exactly one pointer over to it, as one indivisible step.
Nobody ever adds a line to a list or deletes one from it — a table's version is a fact that gets written once and left alone.
Now suppose a reader grabs hold of one particular version and commits to reading only that one.
While it's still working through that data, a completely different writer finishes a brand new commit. Does the reader ever catch wind of that change?
answer: Never. What it pinned stays exactly what it reads, no matter what else happens to the table in the meantime.
It only sees something different if it deliberately goes back and asks for the current version again.

lines: This was tested directly, not just asserted. A reader grabs a version and reads it. Somewhere else, for real, a second writer finishes a commit.
Go back and read that exact same pinned version again, and it comes back byte for byte identical to the very first read.
Notice what writers get to do before any of this matters: stage their new files with absolutely no coordination, no lock, nothing blocking them.
The only moment any race even exists is the instant of the commit itself — and losing that race just means trying again.
So here's that exact race, run for real. Two separate writers both try to claim the very same commit slot, starting from the same base.
One of them genuinely succeeds. The other gets a real failure back immediately, and goes and tries again against whatever just became current.
It's worth knowing this isn't one project's clever trick. A completely separate table format — Delta — describes its own history the exact same way.
One single, ordered sequence of versions, and readers that follow a log instead of ever asking a storage system what files happen to be sitting around.
Pull it together and the whole design is three ideas. A version, once written, is never touched again.
Advancing to a new version is one indivisible swap. And when two writers go for that same swap at once, precisely one of them gets to win.
